Post 1 announces the study; post 2 states the argument, ported near-verbatim from the certified reading-club-islamic-dilemma.html hero (line 241); post 3 carries the author credit and the book recommendation. THREE THINGS A REVIEWER SHOULD CHECK BY NAME. (1) THE AUTHOR-APPROVAL CLAIM IS OWNER-SUPPLIED, NOT REPO-VERIFIED — the page itself says only that Christopher Frost 'has given his permission for this study to be published'; that he has SEEN and APPROVED it comes from the owner and is stated here on their authority. Splitting virtue from content was the adjudication; do not let a compressed post re-merge them. (3) THE BOOK RECOMMENDATION IS AN ENDORSEMENT IN OUR OWN VOICE and is deliberately bounded to what docs/book-research/islamic-dilemma.md actually verifies from a cover-to-cover read — that it is built from the Qur'an itself and routes the reader to mainstream Islamic-studies scholarship (Reynolds, Sinai, Griffith, Whittingham, Nickel, Witztum) — and NOT to its triumphalist claims, which that note names as 'exactly the tone our content must NOT adopt (1 Peter 3:15)'. Post 2 keeps the page's own bounded register ('lay out that tension and ask what it means'), which is where five gate rounds landed; do not harden it into a verdict the certified surface does not state. New from Apologia Daily: a free 16-session reading club for The Islamic Dilemma by Christopher W. Frost (@SCApologia).

Chris has seen the study and approved it. The summaries, questions and judgements are ours, not his; nothing reproduces his text.

https://apologiadaily.com/reading-club-islamic-dilemma.html

The argument:

The Qur'an speaks warmly of the Torah and the Gospel — calling them revelation from God, "guidance and light," and telling Jews and Christians to follow them.

Yet it also contradicts them on central points, from the crucifixion of Jesus to the fatherhood of God.

What makes Frost's book worth your money: he works through the Qur'an itself, not from Christian premises, and he footnotes you out to mainstream Islamic-studies scholarship.

Buy the book. It is all the club needs — our sessions just walk alongside it.

Then read it with someone.

Each session has discussion questions, and the optional Apologia Daily deep-dives are clearly marked as ours and entirely skippable.

The aim is not to win an argument. It is to lay the tension out honestly, and talk it over kindly. (1 Peter 3:15)
